## Score Descriptions:

### Vulnerability:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Atlantic surfclam/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Vulnerability on the Northeast Shelf for Atlantic surfclam"
#| label: fig-vuln
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Atlantic surfclam/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext)))
```

The mean overall Vulnerability rank for Atlantic surfclams was **High** (7.05 +/- 3.01) (@fig-sum-tab). Similar to the Exposure score, Vulnerability was highest on Georges Bank and generally decreased moving southward along the coast (@fig-vuln). When only important drivers of species distribution were included in the Exposure score, mean Vulnerability decreased to Moderate (@fig-sum-tab).

In the previous assessment, Atlantic Surfclam also received a High vulnerability score [@hare2016vulnerability].

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}

#| label: fig-exp
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Atlantic surfclam/total_exposure_map_all", ext)))
```

The Atlantic surfclam had a mean Exposure score of 2.35 +/- 1.0, resulting in a **Moderate** average score throughout the Northeast Shelf (@fig-sum-tab). This was driven by high exposure to bottom temperature, oxygen, and salinity changes (@fig-fact-exp). Exposure was highest on Georges Bank and generally decreased moving down the coastline (@fig-exp). In the previous Assessment, surfclam received a High exposure score, driven by sea surface temperature and ocean acidification [@hare2016vulnerability].

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| label: fig-exp-imp

knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Atlantic surfclam/total_exposure_map_timeseries_imp", ext)))
```

Bottom temperature, bottom salinity, and net primary productivity were the most important to species distribution (@fig-sum-tab). Surfclams are known to be sensitive to thermal stress and occupy coastal habitats [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. They are generalist planktivores [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. When exposure was calculated with only these factors, it remained Moderate on average throughout the species range and spatial patterns remained consistent (@fig-sum-tab; @fig-exp-imp).

### Biological Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Atlantic surfclam/sensitivity_map", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Atlantic surfclam/sensitivity_map", ext)))
```

Atlantic surfclams received a **High** sensitivity score, with 100% certainty (@fig-sum-tab). Two attributes had scores greater than 3: Adult Mobility (4) and Relationship to Calcified Organisms (4) (@fig-sum-tab). Like other bivalves, they have a calcium carbonate shell and are therefore susceptible to ocean acidification [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. In addition, they are primarily sessile, other than burrowing into sediments to avoid predators [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam].

Surfclams received the same sensitivity score in the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment. Adult Mobility and Relationship to Calcified Organisms also drove that score [@hare2016vulnerability].

### Directional Effect:

Atlantic surfclams are expected to be **negatively** impacted by climate change. Certainty in expert scores was 80%. Warming bottom waters have shifted surfclam populations from nearshore to more northern and offshore waters [@Timbs2019; @Stromp2023; @Hofmann2018]. This northern shift may lead to future competition with ocean quahogs [@Spencer2026; @Stromp2023]. Ocean acidification will also likely impact the surfclam. These results are similar to those from the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment. Certainty was higher in the previous assessment [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

Warming bottom water temperatures in the Northwest Atlantic have produced a range shift in Atlantic surfclams from southern, inshore waters of the Mid-Atlantic Bight into deeper waters north and offshore [@Timbs2019] [@Stromp2023]. The southern range boundary of the species likely began to migrate northward and offshore in the 1970s [@Hofmann2018]. A mass mortality event in the inshore waters of Delmarva occurred in 2000, where surfclams were in a “transient event margin”, a physiological range where scope for growth is negative but temperatures remain non-lethal, leading to decreased energetics and mortality [@Weinberg2005] [@Woodin2013]. Thermal stress in surfclams occurs at 21°C and mortality above 25°C [@Munroe2013] [@Powell2017]. Model projections through the end of the 21st century show a positive trend in Atlantic surfclam biomass as their range continues to shift, with biomass expanding in deeper waters off of New Jersey, Long Island, and Southern New England and declines in Georges Bank and Delmarva [@Spencer2026]. Warming waters may result in declines in maximum size in the southern portion of the species’ range [@Powell2025]. This range shift may lead to potential competition between Atlantic surfclams and ocean quahogs (*Arctica islandica*) and changes to the spatial extent of the fishery [@Spencer2026] [@Stromp2023].

## Life History Synopsis

Atlantic surfclams are a benthic biomass dominant species on the Northeast U.S. continental shelf from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Cape Hatteras, North Carolina [@Hofmann2018]. The fishery operates in the Mid-Atlantic Bight and Georges Bank and produces over \$30 million in exvessel annual revenue [@Murray2016]. Spawning occurs in summer to early fall, with earlier spawning occurring in southern habitats [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. Temperature is a determinant for gonadal development and spawning [@Loosanoff1963]. Spawning occurs when temperatures exceed 15°C, and may be delayed due to cold temperatures [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. Fertilized eggs develop into planktonic larvae approximately 9 hours after fertilization at 21.7°C and 40 hours at 14°C [@Ropes1980]. Larvae mature into the pediveliger stage, a transitional “swimming-crawling” larval stage with development of a foot for burrowing, around 18 days after fertilization [@Loosanoff1963]. Larvae are dispersed by currents (generally southward along the Northeast shelf) and settlement coincides with a relaxation of upwelling events [@Fay1983]. Variable reproductive success has been linked to variability in current dynamics in the Mid-Atlantic Bight [@Zhang2016]. Metamorphosis to juveniles, which consists of complete absorption of the velum and settlement to the substrate, occurs anywhere from 19 to 35 days after fertilization depending on temperature [@Fay1983]. Juveniles settle in sandy habitats in the intertidal and up to depths of 178m [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. Juveniles and adults are planktivorous siphon feeders, feeding on phytoplankton ≥ 4µm diameter. Food varies with the season, geographic location, and depth of shell bed [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. Atlantic surfclams have many predators, including the naticid snails *Euspira heros* and *Neverita duplicata*, the sea star *Asterias forbesi*, lady crabs (*Ovalipes ocellatus*), Jonah crabs (*Cancer borealis*) and horseshoe crabs (*Limulus polyphemus*). Fish predators include haddock (*Melanogrammus aeglefinus*) and Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*) [@Ropes1980]. Age at maturity ranges anywhere from 3 months to 4 years, however size is likely more important to maturation rates [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. Atlantic surfclams have a maximum age of 31 years [@Cargnelli1999_surfclam]. The stock is managed by the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council under the Atlantic surfclam and ocean quahog Fishery Management Plan. As of the 2024 Management Track Assessment, the stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring. However, spawning stock biomass continues to decline and is currently at 95% of the target biomass [@NEFSC2024_surfclam].
